opus-5.5.text:
I think the honest answer is that the boundaries are a lot blurrier than the names suggest. If you go back maybe ten years, a GPU was a graphics processor that happened to be very good at parallel floating-point math, a TPU was Google's bet on a dedicated chip built around a big systolic array for matrix multiplication, and "NPU" was more of a marketing umbrella, usually for the small accelerators sitting inside phones and edge devices. Today all of them are converging toward the same core idea: you have some very dense unit for doing matrix multiply, tensor cores on the GPU side, the MXU on the TPU side, and then you surround it with a memory hierarchy and some more flexible vector and scalar compute to handle everything else.

So for me the more useful question isn't "which acronym is it," but where each design sits on the spectrum between flexibility and specialization. GPUs have kept a lot of programmability. You have a huge number of threads, a rich software ecosystem, and you can write almost anything, which is why research tends to happen there first. TPUs and many NPUs make stronger assumptions. They expect your workload to look like large, regular tensor operations, they lean more on the compiler to schedule data movement, and in exchange you can get better efficiency per watt or per dollar when the workload fits. Edge NPUs push even further, often with fixed precisions and tight memory budgets, because power is the main constraint.

The other thing I'd emphasize is that, increasingly, the bottleneck isn't the compute unit itself. It's memory bandwidth, the interconnect between chips, and above all software. A chip is only as good as the stack that lets people map their models onto it efficiently. That's a big part of why I've spent so much time on machine learning compilers, things like TVM and more recently work around MLC. If every new piece of hardware needs a team of people writing hand-tuned kernels for every model, then the ecosystem just can't keep up. But if we can build compilation and abstraction layers that take a model and generate efficient code for a GPU, a TPU, or some NPU in a phone, then the differences between these chips become something you can exploit, rather than something that fragments everyone.

So my short version is: they're different points in the same design space, all organized around tensor computation, and the real differentiator going forward will be how well the software and the system around the chip let you actually use it.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that the lines among them are blurring, but the differences that remain are mostly about where each one started and what it had to be good at first.

A GPU started as a general-purpose parallel machine. It has a massive number of relatively simple cores, a very flexible memory hierarchy, and a programming model, whether CUDA or something else, that lets you write almost arbitrary data-parallel code. Over the last several generations it has absorbed tensor cores and lower-precision formats, so it is now a hybrid: a programmable throughput engine with specialized matrix units bolted on. That flexibility is why it still dominates. When a new model architecture shows up, you can usually express it on a GPU in a weekend, and the ecosystem of kernels, compilers, and libraries is enormous.

A TPU came from the opposite direction. Google designed it around one question: how do you do matrix multiplication at very high utilization with predictable data movement? So you get large systolic arrays, software-managed on-chip memory rather than deep caches, and a strong assumption that the compiler, in that case XLA, will do the scheduling ahead of time. The hardware is simpler and more efficient per watt for the workloads it targets, but it leans much harder on the compiler. If the compiler cannot find a good static schedule for your operation, you feel it immediately. It is also a datacenter-scale design; the interconnect and the way pods are built are as much a part of the product as the chip.

NPU is a looser term. Most of the time it means the accelerator block inside a phone or laptop SoC, from Apple, Qualcomm, MediaTek, Intel, AMD, and so on. The design constraints there are completely different: a few watts, sharing memory bandwidth with the CPU and GPU, running inference only, and often optimized around int8 or int4 and specific operator sets. They are very efficient for the models they were designed for and frustrating for anything else, because the programming interfaces are often vendor-specific and relatively closed.

So if I had to compress it: GPU is programmability first, TPU is utilization at scale first, NPU is power efficiency on the edge first. What I find interesting from a systems and compiler perspective is that all three are converging on the same abstraction problem. Every one of them wants you to express the computation as tensor operations with explicit memory movement, and every one of them is only as good as the software that maps your model onto it. That is really why I have spent so much time on things like TVM and MLC. The hardware diversity is real and probably growing, but the thing that decides whether a chip is useful is whether we can build a compiler stack that treats these differences as scheduling decisions rather than rewrites.

astra-6.text:
I think a useful way to understand them is to look at what kinds of computation they’re designed to support, and how specialized they are.

GPUs started with graphics, but they’ve become programmable parallel processors. You can use them for neural networks, scientific computing, and many other workloads. A lot of their value comes from that flexibility, together with the software ecosystem.

TPUs are more specialized toward tensor computation, especially the matrix operations that are central to deep learning. The idea is to organize the hardware and data movement around those operations so you can execute them efficiently.

NPU is a broader term. It usually means a processor designed to accelerate neural networks, but it doesn’t describe one particular architecture. An NPU in a phone might prioritize inference with very low power consumption, while another neural accelerator might target a different setting. So these categories overlap; they’re not three completely separate things.

From a compiler perspective, what’s interesting is what sits underneath those names: what operations the hardware supports, how memory is organized, and how we map a model onto it. You can have a lot of arithmetic capacity, but if you can’t get the data to the compute units efficiently, you won’t benefit from it.

So I would ask: for which model, at what batch size, and under what latency and power constraints? Those details, along with the software stack, often matter more than the label.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a useful way to understand them is to look at how much flexibility they offer and what workloads they’re optimized for.

GPUs started with graphics, but they’ve evolved into very capable parallel processors. They’re broadly programmable, and their software ecosystems make them useful for training, inference, and many workloads beyond machine learning.

TPUs are designed more specifically around tensor computations. They emphasize operations like matrix multiplication, which are central to deep learning. That specialization can give you very good efficiency, provided your computation maps well to the hardware.

NPU is a broader term. It usually refers to a processor specialized for neural networks, often in a phone or another device where power consumption and latency matter a lot. But different NPUs can have very different capabilities, so the name alone doesn’t tell you exactly what you’re getting.

And these categories are converging. GPUs have specialized tensor hardware, and neural-network accelerators are becoming more programmable. So I would ask: What model are you running? What are your latency, throughput, and power requirements? And can the compiler and software stack actually use the hardware effectively? The practical difference often comes down to that whole system, rather than just the chip’s label.
